directAnswer: St. Gelasius I was pope from 492 to 496 and one of the most important theologians among the early popes. In a letter to Emperor Anastasius I he set out the classic distinction between the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers. Ancient sources describe him as African by birth, and he was the last pope known to have been born on that continent.

sections.h2: The Two Powers: Gelasius's Letter to Anastasius
paras: In 494 Gelasius wrote to Emperor Anastasius I in Constantinople. The letter, known by its opening words Duo sunt, explained that the world is governed chiefly by two powers: the consecrated authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers.

Gelasius told the emperor that, while bishops obey imperial laws in temporal matters, rulers must submit to bishops in what concerns the sacraments and salvation, and that the responsibility of priests is weightier because they must answer to God even for kings. The letter became a foundational text for medieval thinking about the relationship between church and state.

sections.h2: Upholding Rome Against the Acacian Party
paras: Gelasius had served as a close adviser to Felix III and drafted many of his letters. As pope he maintained the excommunication of the late Acacius and refused to remove his name from the Roman condemnations, even as Anastasius pressed for compromise.

He wrote extensively on the question, insisting that the Roman see had the right to judge appeals from all churches and was itself judged by no one. Records of a Roman synod in 495 show the clergy hailing him as Vicar of Christ, one of the earliest such uses of the title for a pope.

sections.h2: Lupercalia, the Eucharist, and Care for the Poor
paras: In Rome, some Christians still took part in the Lupercalia, a pagan February festival. Gelasius wrote against a senator who defended it and worked to end Christian involvement, and the festival disappears from the record after his time.

Finding that Manichaeans in Rome refused to drink from the chalice, he ordered that Communion be received under both kinds, so as to expose and exclude their practice. He wrote theological treatises against Eutyches and Nestorius and set times for ordinations in a letter to bishops of southern Italy.

He used church resources to feed the poor during a period of shortage under Theodoric's new Ostrogothic rule. The Gelasian Sacramentary and the Decretum Gelasianum carry his name, but scholars regard both as later compilations. Gelasius died on November 21, 496.

keyFacts: Pope from 492 to 496; described as African by birth
Wrote the letter Duo sunt (494) on the two powers of bishops and rulers
Maintained the condemnation of Acacius during the Acacian schism
Opposed Christian participation in the pagan Lupercalia

faqs.question: What is Gelasius I's doctrine of the two powers?
faqs.answer: In his 494 letter to Emperor Anastasius, Gelasius taught that the world is governed by the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power of rulers, with rulers subject to bishops in matters of faith and sacraments.

faqs.question: Did Pope Gelasius I write the Gelasian Sacramentary?
faqs.answer: No. The sacramentary is named after him, but scholars date its compilation to later centuries. The same is true of the Decretum Gelasianum, a list of accepted and rejected books.

faqs.question: Was Pope Gelasius I the last African pope?
faqs.answer: He is the last pope known to have been born in Africa. The Liber Pontificalis calls him African, though some scholars think he may have been born in Rome to African parents.
